items.title: Evolution Explains Morality but Cannot Justify It | Alex Rosenberg
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*If evolution explains why we believe something is right or wrong, does that make the belief morally justified?*

Philosopher Alex Rosenberg explains how natural selection could produce cooperation, altruism, and competing moral systems, while arguing that their evolutionary origins cannot establish which morality is objectively correct. For Rosenberg, science can explain our ethical judgments, but it cannot turn facts about nature into moral obligations.

0:00 Grounding Ethics Versus Explaining Altruism
1:13 How Natural Selection Produces Cooperation
3:38 Why Science Cannot Justify a Moral Code
5:28 Competing Moralities as Evolutionary Adaptations
7:02 No Point of View to Adjudicate

*Alexander Rosenberg* is an American philosopher and novelist. He is the R. Taylor Cole Professor of Philosophy at Duke University, well known for contributions to philosophy of biology and philosophy of economics. Rosenberg describes himself as a "naturalist."

items.title: What Happens After Death According to Hinduism? | Swami Sarvapriyananda
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*When the body dies, what exactly continues into another life?*

Swami Sarvapriyananda explains how Hindu philosophy connects karma, reincarnation, and the subtle body, using the image of sunlight reflected in pots of water to distinguish individual consciousness from the true Self. He also explores different experiences of time between lives and why Advaita Vedanta ultimately seeks freedom from the entire cycle of rebirth.

0:00 Karma and the Reason for Reincarnation
1:18 The Atman, Subtle Body, and Rebirth
2:56 What Happens to the Subtle Body at Death
5:01 Different Realms and Timescales Between Lives
6:49 From Resurrection to Liberation From Samsara

*Swami Sarvapriyananda* is a Hindu monk of the Ramakrishna Order and head of the Vedanta Society of New York. He is a prominent teacher of Vedanta and has spoken internationally on Hindu philosophy, spirituality, and interfaith dialogue.

items.title: Can Cognitive Science Test What Art Teaches Us? | W. Christopher Stewart
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:

W. Christopher Stewart explores how cognitive science might investigate the effects of artistic engagement on moral and spiritual formation, and considers the possibility that some realities may be understood better, or perhaps only, through the arts. He emphasizes that demonstrating these effects, especially their underlying causes, remains a difficult challenge.

items.title: Does God Explain Design or Create a Bigger Mystery? | Bede Rundle
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*Does explaining the complexity of life through a divine designer actually explain anything?*

Philosopher Bede Rundle revisits David Hume's challenge to the argument from design: introducing God may add an even more puzzling entity to the explanation. He contrasts this with Darwinian evolution and questions whether describing God as infinitely simple makes the divine hypothesis more intelligible.

0:00 Why the Design Argument Seems Persuasive
1:40 Hume's Objection to a Divine Designer
2:58 Evolution as an Alternative Explanation
3:55 The Limits of Evolutionary Explanation
4:53 Why Divine Simplicity Does Not Advance Understanding

*Bede Rundle* (1937–2011) was a New Zealand-born philosopher and Lecturer Emeritus in Philosophy at the University of Oxford. His research focused on philosophy of language, metaphysics, philosophy of mind, and philosophical theology, particularly questions concerning existence, meaning, and why there is something rather than nothing.

items.author: Closer To Truth

Andrew M. Davis explains Alfred North Whitehead's view that becoming is more fundamental than measurable time. In this process-based account of reality, the past is settled, the future remains genuinely open, and temporal order emerges through the relationships among events.

*Andrew M. Davis* is a philosopher, theologian, and scholar of world religions, and Program Director of the Center for Process Studies at Claremont School of Theology. His work focuses on process philosophy, interreligious studies, and promoting cross-cultural understanding and religious literacy.

items.title: Consciousness Is a Process, Not a Thing | Iain McGilchrist
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*What if consciousness is not something the brain produces, but something fundamental to reality itself?*

Neuroscientist Iain McGilchrist describes consciousness as an evolving encounter rather than an isolated substance. He argues that science can investigate its relationship to brain activity but cannot reveal its intrinsic nature, because consciousness is already the foundation of scientific inquiry.

2:57 Consciousness as the Ground of an Evolving Cosmos

*Iain McGilchrist* is a psychiatrist, neuroscientist, philosopher, and literary scholar, and a former Fellow of All Souls College, Oxford. His interdisciplinary research explores brain hemispheric differences, consciousness, psychiatry, and the relationship between the mind, culture, and human experience.

items.title: The Hidden Assumption Behind Conscious AI | Robert Lawrence Kuhn | Àlex Gómez-Marín
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*In a first for Closer To Truth, the roles are reversed: Àlex Gómez-Marín interviews Robert Lawrence Kuhn, the creator and host of the series.*

*If computational functionalism is correct, could AI become conscious within the next 20–25 years?*

Robert Lawrence Kuhn explains why the possibility of conscious machines depends on which theory of consciousness is correct, while acknowledging that he would bet against computational functionalism. He also reflects on humanity’s capacity to contemplate eternity, explicitly framing his hope for its significance as an emotional argument rather than a scientific or philosophical one.

0:00 AI Consciousness Among Humanity's Ultimate Questions
1:28 Why AI Consciousness Depends on a Theory
3:05 The Assumption of Computational Functionalism
5:47 Why Robert Is Not a Transhumanist
7:04 Contemplating Eternity as an Emotional Argument

*Robert Lawrence Kuhn* is the creator, executive producer, writer, and host of Closer To Truth, which has featured more than 500 leading scientists, philosophers, and creative thinkers in more than 5,000 videos and more than 350 public television episodes on PBS stations. He holds a PhD in anatomy/neuroscience from the UCLA Brain Research Institute and an MBA from MIT's Sloan School of Management. He is the author or editor of more than 30 books, including The Mystery of Existence: Why Is There Anything At All? (with John Leslie), and the author of the Landscape of Consciousness, a taxonomy of more than 500 theories of consciousness.

*Àlex Gómez-Marín* is a Spanish physicist turned neuroscientist. He holds a PhD in theoretical physics and a Masters in biophysics from the University of Barcelona. He was a research fellow at the EMBL-CRG Centre for Genomic Regulation and at the Champalimaud Centre for the Unknown in Lisbon. His research spans from the origins of the arrow of time in inert systems, to the neurobiology of action-perception in living organisms such as flies, worms, mice, and humans.

items.title: Why Language Alone Cannot Establish AI Consciousness | Thomas Nagel
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*Can an AI truly experience anything just because it can talk like a human?*

Thomas Nagel contrasts an AI saying "I'm thirsty" with a human saying the same words: only the human has learned them through experiences independently linked to physical feelings. He considers today's language-based AI an implausible candidate for consciousness, but does not rule out artificial beings that could genuinely interact with the world.

0:00 Why Nagel Calls Claims of Conscious AI Ridiculous
1:30 Why Language Alone Is Not Evidence of Consciousness
4:12 Embodied AI and Interaction With the World
7:33 Consciousness Depends on the Underlying Theory
9:29 The Turing Test Does Not Establish Consciousness

*Thomas Nagel* is an American philosopher and Professor of Philosophy and Law at New York University. His work focuses on philosophy of mind, ethics, and political philosophy, and he is especially known for his influential critique of reductionist accounts of consciousness.

Congratulations to Thomas Nagel, the 2026 laureate of the Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture!

items.title: Who Is the One Experiencing Consciousness? | Acharya Prashant
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*Can we understand consciousness without first asking who is conscious?*

Acharya Prashant challenges Western theories of consciousness by distinguishing scientific explanations of the brain from spiritual self-knowledge. He explores how the ego shapes perception, why intellectual inquiry may fail to examine its own motives, and how our tendency to classify other beings as conscious or unconscious reflects human-centered assumptions.

0:00 Western Theories of Consciousness and Vedic Self-Knowledge

items.title: How Nature Might Point Toward God | C. Stephen Evans
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*Could the natural world provide signs of God without offering definitive proof of God's existence?*

C. Stephen Evans explores how beauty, morality, and the apparent order of nature might lead people toward belief in God. Through his two Pascalian principles, he examines why knowledge of God might be widely accessible yet easy to resist, and how natural signs could connect religious belief with philosophical reasoning.

items.title: Why God May Be Beyond Human Understanding | Alex O'Connor (Part 16 of 19)
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*How can we define God if God is something that exceeds every human concept and description?*

Alex O'Connor explores the difficulty of describing God, the meaning of worship, and the possibility that religious experience reaches beyond what philosophical language can express. Comparing Abrahamic and Eastern traditions, pantheism, and physicalism, he examines whether different conceptions of God point toward the same ultimate reality.

items.title: How Evolution Shaped Our Moral Sense | Nathan Lents
items.author: Closer To Truth
items.content:
<article>*Why would evolution favor people who help others who may never repay them?*

Nathan Lents explores how human morality may have emerged from empathy, cooperation, and the evolutionary advantages of living in supportive groups. He argues that compassion need not depend on calculating personal rewards and explains why broadly generous instincts may have helped early human communities survive.

0:00 Morality Begins With Cognitive Empathy
1:48 Beyond Bookkeeping Reciprocity
2:55 Why Caring Groups Tend to Win
4:26 Group Selection and the Enforcement of Fairness
6:00 Keeping the Instinct Vague

*Nathan H. Lents* is an American scientist, author, and university professor. He has been on the faculty of John Jay College since 2006 and is currently the director of the Cell and Molecular Biology program and the former head of the honors program and the campus Macaulay Honors College program.
